When I finally turned toward myself

There was a morning when I realised the world
was not asking me to hold it all.

The light came in quietly,
touching the edges of the room,
and for the first time in a long while,
I felt something soften inside my own chest —
a small surrender,
like a tired bird laying down its wings.

I had spent years leaning toward others,
offering warmth, carrying weight,
forgetting that my own body was also a place
that needed tending.

So I placed a hand there —
gently, without urgency — and waited.
At first, nothing. Then a single breath rose to meet my palm,
as if my heart had been waiting for this permission.

It was enough. Enough to know that care does not diminish
when turned inward.
Enough to know that kindness is not a river that runs dry
when it circles back to its source.

That day, I walked a little slower.
I loosened the grip on all the invisible bundles I had been carrying for years.
And when the old guilt rose — the familiar whisper
that self-care was selfish — I let it pass
like a shadow moving across water.

The truth was quieter and deeper:
I am allowed to rest. I am allowed to receive.
I am allowed to be held by my own hands.

And the world did not collapse. It didn’t even tremble.
It simply opened a little wider as I stepped back into myself —
not to escape anyone, but to belong to my own life
in the same way I had always belonged to others.

title: Poem - Learning to stay
body:
[fusion_builder_container type="flex" hundred_percent="no" equal_height_columns="no" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" background_position="center center" background_repeat="no-repeat" fade="no" background_parallax="none" parallax_speed="0.3" video_aspect_ratio="16:9" video_loop="yes" video_mute="yes" border_style="solid"][fusion_builder_row][fusion_builder_column type="1_1" layout="1_1" background_position="left top" border_style="solid" border_position="all" spacing="yes" background_repeat="no-repeat" margin_top="0px" margin_bottom="0px" animation_speed="0.3" animation_direction="left" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" center_content="no" last="true" hover_type="none" background_blend_mode="overlay" first="true"][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

Learning to stay

I thought love meant leaning forward,
holding tighter,
keeping the flame alive with my own breath.

I thought if I softened my grip everything might disappear—
that closeness was something you earned by never resting.
But the body knew better.

It grew tired of reaching into the dark,
tired of listening for footsteps that were never promised.
One day I sat still long enough
to feel my own weight arrive.

The spine rose gently,
not to impress anyone,
just to remember it belonged to the earth.
The heart did not close - it widened.

I placed a hand on my chest as if greeting a shy animal,
and for the first time I did not ask it for anything.

I said: You can stay.
You don’t have to chase.
You don’t have to disappear into another body to be real.
Something loosened then— not love,
but the fear around it.

I learned this slowly: connection does not require collapse,
and intimacy does not ask us to abandon our own name.
Now I stand here,
rooted, breathing, open.

I let closeness come when it comes.
I let space remain when it needs to.

And in that kindness—
quiet, unremarkable, true—
I finally feel how deeply
I have always been held.

A Poem a day – 29 December

A poem to read — audio included if you prefer.

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Poem_29_December.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

The Silent Teacher

The year stands almost complete now,
like a path seen from a little distance,
its turns no longer demanding explanation.

Across fields and roads and quiet rooms,
time has been moving all along,
collecting moments without asking which ones mattered most.

Some days were loud and insistent,
others barely marked themselves at all,
yet each left something behind.

Not lessons exactly —
more like traces.
Ways of seeing that were not there before.

The landscape remembers this kind of passing.
Leaves fall without regret.
Water moves on without needing to keep a record.

Even the bare branches carry evidence
of seasons lived through,
not as stories,
but as shape.

Looking back now does not require judgement.
There is no need to gather the year into a single meaning.
It was made of many moments,
each complete in its own way.

Some taught through effort.
Some through waiting.
Some through simply being endured.

What has passed does not vanish.
It settles quietly into what comes next,
informing it without instruction.

The year has been a teacher
not because it tried to be,
but because it happened.

And standing here, close to its end,
there is room to acknowledge that
every moment — even the unnoticed ones —
has already done its work.

A poem to read — audio included if you prefer.

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Poem_30_December.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

I am here

The year comes to its end quietly,
not as a conclusion,
but as a pause where looking back becomes possible.

Twelve months have passed through weather and rooms,
through ordinary days and difficult ones,
through moments that stayed
and moments that barely announced themselves.

Some parts of this year asked a great deal.
They did not arrive gently,
and they did not leave quickly.

There were times when moving forward
meant simply continuing,
without clarity,
without reassurance.

And still —
here you are.

Not unchanged,
but present.
Able to stand at the edge of this year
and see it through.

There is something worth acknowledging in that.
Not triumph.
Not perfection.
Just endurance.

The year offered its teaching
in many forms —
through effort,
through waiting,
through loss,
through quiet persistence.

Even the hardest moments
carried something forward,
whether recognised at the time or not.

Gratitude does not erase what was difficult.
It sits alongside it.
A steady recognition
that being here now
matters.

To see the end of this year
is not something to take lightly.
It means you stayed.
You lived the days that arrived.
You allowed time to move through you.

And as this year closes,
there is space to appreciate that simple fact:

You are here.
You made it to the end.
And that, in itself,
is worth honouring.

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Poem_31_December_The-year-turns.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Last day of the Year

The year is almost finished
and the light knows it.

It moves more slowly now,
rests longer on the hedges,
leans against the bare branches
as if there is no need to hurry.

Nothing is asking to be solved.

What has been lived
does not need to be carried forward
in the same way.

Some things will stay —
the shape of a path,
the way the body remembers water,
the quiet skill of having endured.

Other things loosen on their own,
like leaves finally releasing
after believing they had to hold.

The future stands open
not as a promise
but as space.

Cold, clear,
wide enough to breathe.

Whatever comes,
weather or silence,
work or surprise,
I do not have to leave myself behind.

I am here.
With me.

The year turns.

Being Here - Poem Day 1

Today I’m beginning something new called Being Here.

Over the coming weeks, I’ll be sharing a daily sequence of short poems. Some days they’ll simply be words to read. Other days they’ll be audio pieces meant to be listened to quietly. There’s no programme to follow, nothing to keep up with, and no expectation to listen every day.

Today’s piece is one of the listening poems.

It’s shared for moments when everything feels too much — when the body feels driven, restless, flooded, or on edge. There’s nothing you need to do with it, and nothing to get right. You can listen with your eyes open or closed, sitting or moving, or let it pass by if today isn’t the day.

You’re welcome to listen once, more than once, or not at all. You’re also welcome to come and go over the coming days. This isn’t a course to complete — it’s an offering of quiet company.

If it’s helpful, I’m glad you’re here.

Warmly,
Per

Being Here - Poem Day 2

Today’s poem is part of Being Here, and it’s one for reading rather than listening (optional audio link at the end).

It sits alongside yesterday’s piece and stays with the experience of when everything feels too much — not to resolve it, but to name it more clearly.

There’s nothing to do with this poem. You don’t need to reflect deeply or take anything from it. You’re welcome to read it once, skim it, come back later, or skip it entirely. 

As always, there are no expectations.
This is simply here if it meets you.

Warmly,
Per

When everything feels too much — Reflecting

There are moments when the world feels crowded from the inside.
Not because something dramatic is happening,
but because there has been no space between things.

Thoughts stack up quickly.
Small concerns arrive already carrying weight.
The day seems to lean forward before it has properly begun.

It can feel as though everything needs attention at once —
messages, decisions, unfinished edges —
even when nothing is urgent on its own.

This kind of overwhelm doesn’t always look chaotic from the outside.
It can exist alongside competence, responsibility, and getting on with things.
Often it’s invisible to everyone except the person living inside it.

There may be a constant sense of readiness,
as if something is about to be required,
even in quiet moments.

It’s easy, in states like this,
to assume something is wrong with you —
that you should be coping better,
that others manage this more easily.

But overwhelm is not a personal failure.
It’s often a sign of accumulation,
of too many moments passing without pause,
of demands arriving faster than they can be felt.

Naming this doesn’t fix it.
It doesn’t resolve anything.

It simply allows the experience to be seen clearly,
without judgement,
and without asking it to be different.

Warmly,
Per

Being Here - Poem Day 3

Today’s poem is another one for reading. (optional audio link at the end).

It widens the view a little, staying with the experience of when everything feels too much and placing it in the context of how life often moves around us.

There’s nothing you need to do with it. You’re welcome to read it briefly, read it slowly, or leave it for another time.

Thank you for being here in whatever way works for you.

Warmly,
Per

When everything feels too much — Noticing

There are times when the pace of life leaves little room between moments.
Days fill themselves quickly.
Transitions blur into one another.

Messages arrive faster than they can be answered.
News, opinions, expectations, information —
all moving at once,
all asking to be taken in.

Even ordinary routines can begin to stack up.
Work, care, responsibility, decisions —
each reasonable on its own,
but relentless when combined.

This isn’t unique to one kind of person.
It happens in busy lives and quiet ones,
in times of change
and in periods that look stable from the outside.

The world has learned to move quickly.
To fill silence.
To reward availability.

In that context, feeling overwhelmed
is not surprising.
It is often a natural response
to living without much space.

Noticing this doesn’t explain everything.
It doesn’t offer solutions.

It simply places the experience
where it belongs —
not as a personal flaw,
but as something shaped by how life is lived.

Seeing that clearly
can change the way the moment is held.

Warmly,
Per

not pulled,
not pushed,
simply finding where it belongs.

slow enough to feel,
steady enough to trust,

not opening wide,
just easing enough
to make room for being here.

spreading from the centre outward,
not rushing,
not needing to go anywhere.

When everything feels too much - Reflecting

When the days keep asking

There are times when life doesn’t overwhelm all at once,
but instead keeps asking —
quietly, persistently, without pause.

One thing follows another.
Responsibilities line up neatly.
There is always something that needs attention.

From the outside, this can look like coping.
Getting through.
Managing what’s required.

Inside, it can feel like never quite arriving.
Like standing in the middle of movement
without a clear place to stop.

Nothing here is dramatic.
There may be no crisis, no emergency,
just the steady weight of continuation.

It’s common, in these moments,
to assume this is simply how things are —
that rest belongs elsewhere,
or later,
or to someone else.

But carrying on without interruption
leaves its own mark.
It shapes how time is felt.
It narrows what’s noticed.

Naming this doesn’t change the pace of life.
It doesn’t remove what needs doing.

It simply acknowledges
what it’s like to keep going
when the days keep asking.

When everything feels too much - Noticing

When the days keep asking

Many parts of modern life are built around continuation.
Deadlines roll into the next set of deadlines.
Care leads to more care.
Tasks reproduce quietly.

There is often no clear signal to stop.
No natural ending to a day.
Just a gradual thinning of attention as things continue.

Efficiency is valued.
Responsiveness is rewarded.
Being available is treated as neutral, sometimes even admirable.

In that context, constant engagement can become normalised.
Busyness stops being noticed.
Fatigue blends into routine.

Even rest can begin to feel purposeful —
something to optimise,
schedule,
or justify.

Seen from a little distance,
it makes sense that many people feel stretched
without being able to name why.

Life doesn’t always arrive as intensity.
Sometimes it arrives as accumulation.

Noticing this doesn’t assign blame.
It doesn’t point to solutions.

It simply places the experience
within the shape of the world it’s happening in,
where continuing has become easy
and stopping has become rare.

When everything feels too much - Reflecting

There are times when it isn’t the present moment
that weighs the most,
but what lies just ahead.

Questions linger without answers.
Plans feel provisional.
Certainty keeps shifting its shape.

Even when today is manageable,
the sense of what might come next
can quietly pull attention forward.

The mind fills the gaps on its own.
Imagining outcomes,
preparing for possibilities,
trying to stay one step ahead.

This doesn’t always feel like fear.
Sometimes it feels like vigilance.
Sometimes like responsibility.
Sometimes like being sensible.

But living with uncertainty for long stretches takes energy.
It asks something of the body,
even when nothing is happening yet.

It’s common, in moments like this,
to tell yourself you should be coping better —
that others seem more settled,
more decisive, more sure.

Yet uncertainty is not a personal shortcoming.
It’s part of living in a world
that doesn’t always show its hand.

Naming this doesn’t make the future clearer.
It doesn’t resolve what’s unknown.

It simply acknowledges the quiet effort of living
while not knowing how things will unfold

When everything feels too much - Noticing

Uncertainty is not evenly distributed, 
but it is widely shared.

Plans change. Systems shift. 
Certainty is offered and withdrawn 
by circumstances far beyond individual control.

Many aspects of modern life require flexibility
 — work, housing, health, relationships, belonging
 — often without clear timelines or guarantees.

In this landscape, 
not knowing what’s next is no longer unusual. 
It’s woven into how things move.

People learn to adapt quietly. 
To hold possibilities open. 
To prepare without assurance.

This kind of ongoing uncertainty 
doesn’t always announce itself as stress. 
It can show up as watchfulness, 
as hesitation, 
as a reluctance to settle into any one direction.

Seen this way, 
feeling unsettled about the future 
is not a sign of personal instability. 
It reflects the conditions 
many lives are shaped within.

Noticing this doesn’t reduce uncertainty. 
It doesn’t promise clarity.
It simply places the experience where it belongs
 — within a world that often asks people to live
 without knowing what comes next.

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-10.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

When I need connection right now

There is space here for wanting.
Nothing about this moment
says you are too much.

The body is already somewhere solid,
supported without being held tightly,
resting without slipping away.

Attention settles into where you are,
not scanning outward,
not searching ahead,
just noticing this place has edges.

Movement slows naturally,
not because it’s asked to,
but because there is nothing pulling it forward.

Breath continues on its own,
arriving and leaving,
not trying to reach anyone,
not needing an answer back.

Warmth stays close to the centre,
steady rather than spreading,
present without leaning.

The chest softens without opening wide.
The hands don’t have to reach.
The body doesn’t have to follow the urge.

The feeling of wanting is allowed to exist,
without being fed and without being pushed away.
Connection doesn’t disappear here.
It simply stops rushing.

There is a sense of being accompanied
without anyone else entering the scene,
a quiet knowing that you
are not alone inside yourself.

This moment does not depend on response.
It does not require closeness to arrive.

You remain here,
held by your own presence,
able to wait without losing contact.
For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 11

Today’s poem stays with a very human moment —
when the need for connection rises quickly, before there’s time to think about it.

This isn’t a poem that tries to soothe or settle anything.
It doesn’t tell the wanting to go away.

Instead, it names what that pull can feel like from the inside —
the warmth, the urgency, the narrowing of attention,
and the way care and fear can arrive together.

Yesterday’s poem worked quietly at the level of the body.
Today’s poem offers recognition.

Nothing here needs to be resolved.
Nothing needs to change.

Sometimes, being able to see an experience clearly —
without judging it or acting on it —
is enough to let it take its rightful place.

The poem is below, exactly as it is meant to be met.

(I have included the audio if you like to hear it as well)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

When I need connection right now - Reflecting

There are moments when 
the need for connection rises quickly. 
Not as a thought, 
but as a pull.

The body notices it first 
— a leaning forward, 
a readiness to reach, 
a sense that something important 
is just out of view.

Attention narrows around the idea of closeness. 
Messages, voices, responses begin to carry more weight than usual.
It can feel physical, this wanting 
— a warmth in the chest, a quickening, 
a subtle urgency that doesn’t wait to be explained.

Often, the mind moves in alongside it. 
Replaying conversations. 
Imagining contact. 
Wondering how to close the distance.

This isn’t neediness in the way it’s often described. 
It’s a human response, 
shaped by care, memory, 
and the wish to belong.

At times, the wanting carries tenderness. 
At other times, it carries fear — 
the sense that without connection, 
something essential might be lost.

In these moments, 
it’s easy to forget that the body itself is already present, 
already containing sensation, 
already holding warmth and movement.

The urge to reach doesn’t mean something is missing. 
It often means something matters.
Seeing this clearly doesn’t quiet the wanting. 
It doesn’t resolve it.

It simply allows the experience to be recognised 
as part of how connection lives in a human system
 — felt in the body, 
imagined in the mind, 
and shaped by care.

Being Here - Poem Day 12

Being Here - Poem Day 12

Today’s poem steps back slightly.

Day 10 poem worked quietly with the body
and Day 11 named the inner experience of wanting
This poem widens the frame.

It looks at the conditions that shape urgency around connection —
how closeness now moves through messages, timing, availability,
and how absence can feel louder than it once did.

Nothing here is meant to settle the longing
or explain it away. The poem doesn’t turn inward.
It doesn’t ask you to reflect on yourself.

It simply places the experience where it belongs —
inside the world relationships now live in.

Sometimes that wider view matters.
Not because it fixes anything,
but because it loosens the idea that this urgency is a personal flaw.

The poem is below, offered as context, not correction.  Sit back, read it, and let it land.  (I have included the audio if you like to hear it as well)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I need connection right now - Noticing

Urgent longing for connection doesn’t arise in isolation.
It takes shape within patterns of contact, distance,
and availability that surround everyday life.

Messages travel instantly now.
Responses can arrive — or not — without explanation.
Presence is often partial,
split across places, screens, and demands.

In this landscape,
wanting connection can intensify quickly.
The absence of reply feels louder.
Delays carry more meaning than they once did.

Care and closeness are no longer tied to physical proximity alone.
They move through signals, timings, tones, and pauses
— all of which can be misread or over-weighted
when connection feels uncertain.

Many people learn to stay alert to these shifts.
To watch for signs of engagement.
To reach sooner rather than later,
just in case the window closes.

Seen this way, urgency around connection is not simply personal.
It reflects the conditions relationships now live within
— fragmented time, shared attention,
and contact that can disappear without warning.

Noticing this doesn’t reduce the wanting.
It doesn’t make closeness easier or harder to reach.
It simply places the experience within the wider context that shapes it,
where the need to connect often has as much to do
with circumstance as with the heart itself.

Being Here - Poem Day 13

Being Here - Poem Day 13

After three days with reaching — when connection feels urgent, necessary, hard to bear alone — today’s poem turns toward the other side of the same human pattern.

When closeness feels like too much.

This is the moment many of us recognise quietly:
when distance isn’t rejection, but protection.
When pulling back is the only way the system knows how to stay intact.

This poem does not ask for openness.
It doesn’t encourage sharing, softening, or moving closer.

It honours withdrawal as intelligence —
while offering a way to stay present inside your own boundary, without disappearing further.

As with Days 10–12, nothing is required. Listening is enough.

You don’t need to decide whether closeness is good or bad.
You don’t need to move toward or away from anyone.

This poem simply offers a place where distance can rest
without becoming loneliness.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-13.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When closeness feels like too much

There is room here to stay as you are. 
Nothing is asking you to move closer.

The body is already held by its own outline, 
contained without pressure, 
separate without being alone.

Awareness settles where you are sitting, 
inside your own space, 
with clear edges and no expectation to open

Muscles soften just enough to rest against themselves, 
not reaching outward, 
not pulling away.

Breath continues quietly, 
uninvolved, not shared, not directed.

The chest remains steady. 
It doesn’t need to widen. 
It doesn’t need to close.

Warmth stays where it belongs, 
close to the centre, 
contained, reassuring in its limits.

Distance is allowed here. 
So is stillness. 
Neither is a problem to solve.

The body recognises that closeness can arrive later, 
or not at all, and nothing essential is lost.

There is a sense of being present without being exposed, 
connected to yourself without being required.

This moment respects your boundary. 
It doesn’t lean in.

You remain here, 
whole within your own space, 
able to stay without retreating further.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 14

Yesterday’s poem, When closeness feels like too much, stayed with the body.It didn’t ask for contact or movement — only allowed distance to be safe.

Today’s poem stays with the experience of that distance.

When closeness feels like too much — Reflecting
is not designed to regulate or settle.
It doesn’t move anything forward.

Instead, it names something many people carry quietly:
that pulling back is often not rejection,
but a way of staying intact when capacity is low.

This poem meets the questions that often follow withdrawal —
the self-judgement, the interpretation, the worry about what it “means” —
and offers a different frame.

Distance can be care.
Timing can matter.
Stepping back does not cancel connection.

There’s nothing to practise here.
Nothing to change.

This poem simply offers language
for recognising what may already be true
when closeness feels like too much.

Gently read it and let it land. (link to adio version below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When closeness feels like too much - Reflecting

There are moments when distance feels easier than closeness. 
Not because connection isn’t wanted, 
but because it asks for more than feels available.

The body may respond first —
 a tightening, a pulling back, 
a preference for space that doesn’t need explanation.

This can happen even with people who matter. 
Even in relationships that feel generally safe. 
Closeness can still arrive as pressure rather than comfort.

Often, the mind steps in with interpretation. 
Questions about what this means. 
Concerns about being cold, withdrawn, or unkind.

But stepping back is not the same as rejecting. 
It’s often a way of staying intact, 
of preserving a sense of self when proximity feels overwhelming.

There may be relief in the space created. 
A quiet steadiness. 
A sense of being able to breathe without being seen too closely.

This doesn’t mean connection is impossible. 
It means timing matters. 
So does capacity.

Recognising this can soften self-judgement. 
It allows distance to be understood as a form of care — 
not just for others, 
but for yourself.

Seeing withdrawal this way 
doesn’t require it to change.
It simply honours what is happening 
when closeness feels like too much.

Being Here - Poem Day 15

Over the last three days, When closeness feels like too much has been approached from three different angles.

Day 13 stayed with the body —
allowing distance to be safe, without asking for change.

Day 14 offered language —
meeting the meaning we often place on withdrawal, and softening self-judgement.

Today’s poem steps back further.

When closeness feels like too much — Noticing
places this experience in a wider context.

It looks at how closeness is shaped by pace, expectation, history, and environment —
by how much space modern life allows,
and by the conditions relationships are lived within.

Distance is not framed as a problem to fix,
nor as a virtue to adopt.

It is simply recognised as one of the ways people stay in relationship
without losing themselves.

There is nothing here to practise or resolve.
This poem doesn’t turn inward.

It widens the frame —
so the experience can rest where it belongs.

Gently read it and let it land. (link to adio version below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When closeness feels like too much - Noticing

Closeness does not happen in a vacuum.
It is shaped by pace, expectation, history,
and by how much space is available in a given moment.

Many environments reward openness, sharing, and responsiveness.
Availability is often taken as a sign of care.
Distance, by contrast, can be misunderstood.

In such settings, stepping back may feel like deviation —
even when it is the most stable response available.

Not everyone has equal capacity for closeness at all times.
Energy fluctuates.
Demands accumulate.
Boundaries shift as circumstances change.

Some people learn early that maintaining space
is the safest way to stay present at all.
Others discover it later,
after closeness has repeatedly arrived as overwhelm.

Seen this way, withdrawal is not absence.
It is a way of managing contact within the limits of what feels tolerable.

Modern life often compresses space.
Homes are shared.
Communication is constant.
Privacy is negotiated rather than assumed.

In that context, needing distance is not unusual.
It reflects the conditions relationships are lived within,
not a failure of connection.

Noticing this doesn’t explain away the experience.
It doesn’t turn distance into a virtue.

It simply places it where it belongs —
as one of the many ways people stay in relationship
without losing themselves.

Being Here - Poem Day 16

After three days with distance —
felt in the body, named in language, and placed in context —
today’s poem turns toward a different experience of connection.

Oscillation.

This is the movement many people recognise:
wanting closeness,
then needing space,
then wanting closeness again.

Not as indecision.
Not as immaturity.

But as a nervous system moving between safety strategies.

Today’s poem is functional.
It works at the level of the body, not meaning.

It doesn’t try to stabilise you into closeness
or push you out of distance.

Instead, it supports staying present
while the system moves back and forth —
without needing to resolve that movement.

As always, nothing is required.
You don’t need to decide what this pattern means,
or where you “should” land.

Listening is enough.

Gently listen to it and let it land. (text included below)

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I want closeness and then don’t

There is space here for movement in both directions. 
Nothing needs to settle into one position.
The body is already present, 
supported where it is, 
able to shift without losing its place.

Attention widens enough to include more than one feeling at a time — 
the pull toward, and the pull away.
Neither needs to win.

The rhythm of this moment is allowed. 
Approach and pause. 
Interest and retreat. 
Each arriving in its own time.

Breath continues without choosing sides, 
moving in, 
moving out, 
not aligning itself with either urge.

Warmth comes and goes gently, 
not flooding, 
not disappearing, 
staying available without insisting.

The chest doesn’t have to open fully or close itself down.
 It can remain responsive, 
adjusting moment by moment.

Wanting is felt without being acted on. 
Distance is felt without being defended.
The body learns that movement itself does not mean danger. 
Shifting does not mean losing contact.

There is a sense of staying with yourself even as feelings change direction, 
a steady presence beneath the motion.
This moment does not require a decision. 
It does not ask you to choose closeness or space.

You remain here, 
inside a body that can move and pause, 
reach and rest, 
without falling apart.

For now, 
that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 17

Today’s poem stays close to the inner experience of connection.

It speaks to those moments when closeness feels inviting, and then suddenly doesn’t — when wanting and hesitating exist at the same time.
Not to explain it away, and not to resolve it, but simply to name it honestly.

There’s nothing here to work out or change.
Just listening can be enough to feel a little less alone with this movement.

As always, let it meet you where it does.

Gently read it and let it land. (audio included below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I want closeness and then don’t - Reflecting

When I want closeness and then don’t — Reflecting
There are moments
when desire moves
in more than one direction
at once.

Closeness feels inviting,
and then suddenly heavy.
Distance feels relieving,
and then unexpectedly lonely.

The shift can happen quickly.
Sometimes without a clear reason.
A moment ago, reaching felt right.
Now it feels like too much.

This movement is often confusing.
It can be hard to explain to others,
and even harder to make sense of internally.

The mind may look for consistency.
A clear preference.
A stable position to stand in.

But lived experience
doesn’t always organise itself that way.
Wanting and hesitating can exist together.
So can care and caution.

There may be moments of warmth
followed by a need to step back.
Moments of missing
followed by a wish for space.

This doesn’t mean something is wrong.
It often means more than one need is present at the same time.
Trying to force clarity can add strain.
So can judging the movement as indecision or failure.

Recognising the oscillation doesn’t require choosing a side.
It simply acknowledges the reality
of moving between closeness and distance.

Seeing this clearly can allow the experience to be held
with a little more honesty
and a little less pressure.

Being Here - Poem Day 18

Today’s poem widens the view on connection.

Rather than staying inside personal experience, it looks at how closeness and distance are shaped by context — time, capacity, interruption, and the pace of modern life.

The coming and going many people feel isn’t framed here as a flaw or confusion, but as something responsive to the conditions relationships are lived in.

There’s nothing to change or resolve.

Just reading and listening to this poem may help the experience feel less personal, and a little more understandable.

Gently read it and let it land. (audio included below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I want closeness and then don’t - Noticing

Many relationships are lived across changing conditions. 
Time, availability, 
emotional capacity, 
and expectation rarely stay constant.

Closeness can be welcomed in one moment and feel intrusive in the next, 
depending on context rather than intention.

Modern life often intensifies this movement. 
Contact is frequent but fragmented. 
Connection happens alongside interruption. 
Distance can appear suddenly, without explanation.

In such conditions, people learn to adjust continually. 
To lean in when it feels possible, 
and pull back when it doesn’t.

This back-and-forth is not always a sign of ambivalence. 
It can be a response to fluctuating demands, 
uneven energy, 
and relationships that require ongoing negotiation.

Some environments allow for this movement. 
Others reward consistency and clarity, 
making oscillation feel like a personal shortcoming.

Seen from a wider view, coming and going is often an adaptation. 
A way of staying in relationship without becoming overwhelmed or depleted.

Noticing this doesn’t make the pattern disappear. 
It doesn’t turn movement into balance.

It simply places the experience within the realities of how connection is lived — 
responsive, shifting, 
and shaped by more than one need at a time.

Being Here - Poem Day 19

Today we begin a new part of the programme.

After working with connection and belonging,
the focus turns toward agency —
the energy of doing, striving, moving things forward.

When I can’t stop pushing forward - 
is a functional poem for moments when momentum has nowhere to land,
when effort keeps going even after direction is clear.

This poem does not ask you to stop caring, slow down permanently,
or give up what matters.

It allows doing to rest inside being, so energy can gather rather than burn through.

As always, nothing is required.
Listening is enough.

Gently listen to it and let it land. (text included below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-19.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I can’t stop pushing forward

There is room here to pause without falling behind. 
Nothing important is lost by being still for a moment.

The body is already supported, 
held by something solid beneath it, 
not needing to brace or lean.

Awareness settles into where you are now, 
not scanning for the next step, 
not calculating what comes after.

Muscles release their constant readiness, 
not giving up strength, 
just resting it where it belongs.

Breath moves without instruction, 
no longer pulled upward by urgency, 
no longer driven by effort.

Warmth gathers steadily, 
not sharp, 
not explosive, 
contained and usable.

The chest softens without collapsing. 
Energy doesn’t disappear — 
it reorganises.

The urge to act is allowed to quiet 
without being silenced. 
Direction remains, 
but it no longer needs to hurry.

The body recognises that movement 
is more effective when it can stop and start, 
rather than push endlessly.

There is a sense of standing inside yourself, 
not ahead of yourself, 
able to feel what is present before deciding what comes next.

This moment does not ask you to quit.
It does not ask you to slow down forever.

It simply allows you to be here, 
with your energy gathered, 
your agency intact, 
and your next step not yet required.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 20

When I can’t stop pushing forward - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked at the level of the body —
meeting relentless forward drive without taking away energy or direction.

Today’s poem stays with the experience of that drive.

When I can’t stop pushing forward — Reflecting - doesn’t try to regulate, settle, or slow anything down.

Instead, it names what sustained effort can feel like from the inside:
the familiarity of readiness,
the sense of purpose,
the pride in competence and follow-through.

It also acknowledges the quieter tensions that can live beneath momentum —
the worry that stopping might cost something,
that pausing could undo what has been held together.

This poem doesn’t argue with the urge to keep moving.
It doesn’t ask it to change.

It simply allows the experience to be recognised
as a meaningful way of staying engaged with life —
one that carries strength, and also its own cost.

As always, nothing is required.
Simply readig the poem and let the words land is enough.

Gently listen to it and let it land. (text included below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I can’t stop pushing forward - Reflecting

There are times when movement becomes the default.
One task leads into the next.
One goal opens onto another.

The body learns the rhythm of effort.
Readiness becomes familiar.
Stopping begins to feel like interruption rather than rest.

From the inside,
this can feel purposeful.
Even necessary.

Pushing forward carries a sense of agency,
of being alive,
of keeping things in motion.

Often there is pride here.
Competence.
A history of getting things done when they need to be done.

And yet, beneath the momentum,
there can be a quiet tension —
the sense that slowing might mean losing something,
that pausing could let things unravel.

It’s not always obvious what’s being protected.
Sometimes it’s direction.
Sometimes relevance.
Sometimes the feeling of being needed.

The drive to keep moving doesn’t come from nowhere.
It’s shaped by expectations,
by responsibility,
by the rewards that follow effort.

Recognising this doesn’t take the energy away.
It doesn’t argue with the urge to act.

It simply allows the experience to be seen as a way of staying engaged with life,
one that carries strength,
and also its own kind of cost.

Seeing that clearly can soften the story told about it —
without asking the momentum to disappear.

Being Here - Poem Day 21

When I can’t stop pushing forward - Noticing

Over the last three days, When I can’t stop pushing forward has been approached from three angles.

Day 19 worked with the body —
allowing forward drive to settle without taking away energy or direction.

Day 20 stayed with inner experience —
recognising effort, competence, and the tensions that can live beneath momentum.

Today’s poem steps back further.

When I can’t stop pushing forward — Noticing
places this experience in a wider context.

It looks at how modern environments are organised around output, pace, and visible progress — how starting is rewarded, while stopping is often left undefined.

In this frame, relentless movement is not treated as a personal flaw or a lack of self-control. It is seen as a response to the conditions many people live and work within,
where slowing down has few external signals of permission.

This poem doesn’t argue with what is required.
It doesn’t offer a solution.

It simply widens the lens, so the experience of pushing forward can rest where it belongs.

As always, nothing is required.
Simply readig the poem and let the words land is enough.

Gently listen to it and let it land. (text included below)

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I can’t stop pushing forward - Noticing

Many environments are built around momentum.
Progress is measured.
Output is visible.
Movement is rewarded.
Starting is encouraged.
Stopping is less clearly defined.

In work, in learning, in care,
there is often more to do than can reasonably be finished.
Completion becomes provisional.
The next demand waits close by.

In these conditions,
pushing forward makes sense.
It aligns with how success is recognised.
It keeps pace with expectations that rarely pause.

Rest can appear optional.
Pausing can feel inefficient.
Stillness may even be mistaken for disengagement.

Over time,
this shapes how agency is lived.
Doing becomes the primary way of staying connected —
to purpose, to value, to belonging.

Seen this way,
relentless movement is not simply personal drive.
It reflects the structures many people operate within,
where slowing down has few external signals of permission.

Noticing this doesn’t remove the pressure to act.
It doesn’t change what is required.

It simply places the experience within a wider pattern,
where pushing forward is often less a choice
and more a response to how life is organised.

Being Here - Poem Day 22

When I can’t stop pushing forward - Noticing

When I can’t get started

We remain within the theme of agency and reward,
but today the focus shifts.

After meeting relentless forward drive, today’s poem turns toward the other side of the same system — the moments when movement doesn’t arrive at all.

When I can’t get started - this is a functional poem for times of low agency:
- when initiative feels distant,
- when action stalls,
- when energy doesn’t gather on demand.

This poem does not motivate.

It does not encourage starting, or suggest that something is wrong.

It works by allowing stillness to be safe, so readiness can emerge without being forced.

Nothing is required.
Nothing needs to be decided.

Listening is enough. Simply listen to the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I can’t get started

There is no rush here to begin.
Nothing is waiting to be proven.
The body is already somewhere real,
supported without needing to gather energy,
allowed to stay exactly where it is.

Attention rests with what’s present,
not searching for momentum,
not looking for a reason to move.

Weight settles gently,
not heavy,
not dragging,
simply placed.

Breath continues quietly,
uninvolved,
arriving and leaving without being asked to change.

Warmth appears slowly,
subtle rather than bright,
enough to be felt without needing to grow.

The chest remains steady.
It doesn’t need to lift.
It doesn’t need to collapse.

Stillness is allowed to be still.
Pausing is not treated as failure.
Nothing is missing from this moment.

The body recognises that readiness is not created by force.
It arrives when there is enough ground to stand on.

There is a sense of being here without pressure to act,
present without needing direction.
This moment does not ask you to start.
It doesn’t ask you to decide.

It simply lets you remain,
inside a body that knows how movement begins when it is time.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 23

When I can’t stop pushing forward - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked quietly with the body —
allowing stillness to be safe when starting feels out of reach.

Today’s poem stays with the experience of that state.

When I can’t get started — Reflecting
does not try to energise, encourage, or explain.

It names what low agency can feel like from the inside:
the flatness,
the absence of urgency,
the sense of being present without momentum.

This poem recognises that difficulty initiating
is not always resistance, avoidance, or lack of will.

Sometimes it is simply where the system is —
after effort, after pressure, after too much demand.

There is nothing here to practise.
Nothing to push through.

Just language for an experience many people carry quietly,
often without much permission to name.

Simply read the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I can’t get started - Reflecting

There are times when beginning feels harder than it should.
Not because the task is unclear,
but because the energy to meet it isn’t there.

The day may stretch out ahead,
full of possibilities,
yet none of them seem close enough to touch.

Motivation is often spoken about as something you either have or don’t.
But lived experience is rarely that simple.

Sometimes the body doesn’t respond to intention.
Plans stay theoretical.
Decisions remain suspended.

This can be frustrating,
especially when there’s an expectation
that wanting something should be enough to make it happen.

It’s easy, in these moments,
to turn the pause into a judgement —
to see stillness as laziness,
or hesitation as failure.

Yet not starting is not always avoidance.
It can be a sign of depletion,
of uncertainty,
or of having moved too fast for too long.

There may be a quiet wish underneath it all —
for clarity,
for direction,
for something to feel worth beginning.

Recognising this doesn’t create momentum.
It doesn’t unlock a next step.
It simply allows the experience of not starting to be seen without pressure,
as part of how agency ebbs and flows over time.

Being Here - Poem Day 24

When I can’t stop pushing forward - Noticing

Day 22 worked with the body — allowing stillness to be safe, without pushing readiness to appear.

Day 23 stayed with inner experience — naming flatness and stalled action without judgement.

Today’s poem steps back further.

When I can’t get started — Noticing places low agency in a wider context.

It looks at how fatigue, saturation, constant demand, and unclear endings
shape the ability to initiate — and how environments that reward output
often leave little space for pause, recovery, or reset.

In this frame, difficulty starting is not treated as laziness or failure.
It is seen as a response to conditions that ask for more than can easily be given.

This poem doesn’t explain the experience away.
It doesn’t turn stillness into a virtue.

It simply widens the lens, so low agency can be understood as part of how lives are lived, not just something happening inside one person.

Simply read the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I can’t get started - Noticing

Periods of low momentum often arise in environments that ask for continual output. 
Energy is expected to be available on demand. 
Initiation is treated as a personal responsibility.

Yet bodies move in cycles. 
Capacity fluctuates. 
Readiness is not constant.

In many settings, 
there is little room for this variation. 
Pacing is externally set. 
Deadlines arrive regardless of internal state.

Under these conditions, 
not starting can become the only available signal that something needs to pause.

This pause is rarely recognised. 
It is more often interpreted as resistance, 
procrastination, 
or lack of will.

Seen more broadly, difficulty initiating may reflect an absence of conditions that support engagement — clarity, safety, meaning, or rest.

Modern life often disconnects action from reward. 
Effort does not always lead to satisfaction. 
Completion does not guarantee relief.

In such contexts, 
the system may slow itself down, 
waiting for something to make beginning feel worthwhile again.

Noticing this doesn’t create movement. 
It doesn’t provide solutions.

It simply places the experience within the wider conditions that shape agency, 
where starting is not always possible until the ground beneath it feels steady enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 25

Whe I want to act and then don't

Over the last six days, agency has been met in different forms —
first when effort couldn’t stop,
then when movement couldn’t begin.

Today’s poem stays with what many people recognise as most familiar:
the movement between.

Starting, then stalling.
Resting, then pushing.
Momentum arriving — and disappearing again.

Day 25 is a functional poem for oscillating agency.
It does not try to stabilise you into action,
and it does not encourage staying still.

Instead, it supports staying present
while readiness and effort come and go —
without needing to resolve that movement.

This poem doesn’t ask you to decide what your “right” level of agency should be.
It doesn’t offer a strategy for balance.

It simply allows the body to experience fluctuation
without treating it as a mistake.

Listening is enough.

Simply listen to the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-25.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I want to act and then don't

There is room here for movement and pause.
Nothing needs to settle into one pace.

The body is already supported,
able to lean forward and to rest back without losing its place.

Awareness widens to include change —
the rise of intention,
the softening of interest,
both arriving honestly.

Energy gathers for a moment,
then releases.
Neither is treated as failure.

Breath continues without aligning itself with starting or stopping,
moving through both without preference.

Warmth shifts subtly,
sometimes brighter,
sometimes quieter,
remaining available throughout.

The chest doesn’t have to commit.
It can stay responsive,
meeting each phase as it comes.

The urge to act is allowed to appear without being forced into completion.
The slowing is allowed without being explained away.

The body learns that fluctuation is not collapse.
Changing direction does not mean losing agency.

There is a sense of staying present through momentum and through pause,
inside the same steady outline.

This moment does not ask for consistency.
It does not ask you to decide who you are in motion.
You remain here,
inside a body that can begin and stop,
try and rest,
without breaking trust with itself.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 26

Whe I want to act and then don't - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked at the level of the body —
allowing agency to move back and forth
without being pushed to settle.

Today’s poem stays with the experience of that movement.

Poem - When starting and stopping keep alternating — Reflecting does not try to smooth out fluctuation or explain how to stabilise it.

Instead, it names what oscillating agency can feel like from the inside:
- moments of readiness followed by loss of momentum,
- energy that appears and then recedes,
- effort that doesn’t follow a straight line.

This can be confusing, sometimes frustrating, often accompanied by self-judgement.

The poem doesn’t correct that experience.
It doesn’t turn fluctuation into a lesson.

It simply allows the movement itself to be recognised as part of how agency is lived — especially under pressure, uncertainty, or fatigue.

Nothing needs to be decided.
Nothing needs to resolve.

Reading the poem is enough.

Simply listen to the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I want to act and then don't - Reflecting

There are moments when intention arrives clearly,
full of energy and possibility.
And then, just as clearly,
it recedes.

The shift can feel confusing.
What seemed important a moment ago loses its urgency.
What felt possible begins to feel distant.

This movement often invites interpretation.
Questions about commitment.
Concerns about follow-through.
Judgements about discipline or resolve.

Yet lived experience is rarely linear.
Motivation doesn’t always travel in straight lines.
Desire and capacity don’t always rise together.

There may be brief surges of clarity followed by a need to stop.
Bursts of interest followed by fatigue or doubt.

Trying to force continuity can create strain.
So can assuming that pause means something has gone wrong.
Often, what’s being navigated is not a lack of will, but competing signals —
the wish to move and the need to rest.

Recognising this doesn’t stabilise the rhythm.
It doesn’t produce consistency.
It simply allows the fluctuation itself to be named honestly,
without turning it into a verdict about who you are.

Being Here - Poem Day 27

When starting and stopping keep alternating — Noticing

Over the last two days, oscillating agency has been met from different angles:

Day 25 worked with the body —
allowing energy and effort to rise and fall
without being pushed to settle.

Day 26 stayed with inner experience —
naming the confusion and self-judgement that often follow inconsistency.

Today’s poem steps back further.

The Poem When starting and stopping keep alternating — Noticing places this fluctuation in a wider context.

It looks at how uncertainty, changing demands, fatigue, and unclear endings
shape the way agency shows up —
how lives organised around pressure and adaptation rarely move in straight lines.

Seen this way, inconsistency is not personal failure.
It reflects conditions that require constant adjustment, where readiness is repeatedly interrupted and re-formed.

This poem doesn’t explain the experience away.
It doesn’t offer a strategy for smoothing it out.

It simply widens the lens, so oscillation can be understood as one of the ways people keep going without burning out or giving up.

Reading the poem is enough.

Simply read the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I want to act and then don't - Noticing

Many systems expect steady output.
Consistency is often treated as reliability.
Variation is less easily accommodated.

Work cycles, social expectations,
and productivity norms tend to favour sustained effort
over rhythms that rise and fall.

Within these structures,
changing momentum can feel out of place.
Starting and stopping may be read as inefficiency rather than adaptation.

Yet bodies do not operate on constant drive.
Energy responds to sleep, stress, meaning,
and to whether effort feels connected to reward.

In environments where outcomes are uncertain
or effort is repeatedly disconnected from satisfaction,
agency may surge briefly and then withdraw.

Seen this way, oscillation is not confusion.
It can be a response to mismatched demands —
a system testing whether movement is worth continuing.

Modern life often compresses timelines.
Decisions are expected quickly.
Follow-through is assumed.

Under these conditions,
fluctuating motivation becomes visible,
and sometimes problematised.

Noticing this doesn’t smooth the pattern.
It doesn’t stabilise energy.

It simply places the experience within the realities that shape agency,
where starting and stopping can be signs
of ongoing negotiation between effort,
meaning, and capacity.

Being Here - Poem Day 28

Poem - When I feel I have to defend myself

Today the programme moves into a new area:
boundaries and fairness.

This part of the work meets moments when boundaries become rigid,
when vigilance rises quickly,
and when protecting what matters can tip into defensiveness or attack.

Day 28 is a functional poem for times when safety feels uncertain
and fairness feels under threat.

It does not ask you to drop your boundaries.
It does not encourage openness, compromise, or softness.

Instead, it supports firmness without attack —
allowing the body to stay grounded and clear
without hardening or bracing.

This poem works at the level of the body, not meaning.
It settles reactivity
without taking away strength or discernment.

As always, nothing is required.

Simply listen to the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I feel I have to defend myself

There is space here to stand without bracing. 
Nothing is coming toward you right now.
The body is already upright, 
supported by what’s beneath it, 
steady without locking itself in place.

Awareness settles into where you are,
inside clear edges, 
not scanning for intrusion, 
not preparing for impact.

Muscles release their tight readiness, 
not dropping protection, 
just easing the constant hold.

Breath moves freely again, 
no longer held at the top, 
no longer pressed down, 
finding its own depth.

Warmth stays contained, 
strong but not sharp, 
present without needing to surge outward.

The chest remains firm and open enough, 
not armoured, 
not exposed, 
able to hold ground without pushing back.

The sense of “mine” becomes clear without becoming rigid. 
What belongs to you stays with you.
 What does not, stays outside.
The body recognises that boundaries do not require force to be real.

There is a feeling of solidity here, 
quiet and reliable, 
where fairness doesn’t need to be defended 
because it is already felt.

This moment does not ask you to confront. 
It does not ask you to withdraw.

You remain here, 
standing inside your own limits, 
able to respond without preparing for battle.

For now, that is enough.

Listening to the poem is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 29

Poem - When I feel I have to defend myself - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked with the body — meeting moments of defensiveness and vigilance without asking boundaries to collapse.

Today’s poem stays with the experience of that state.

When I feel I have to defend myself — Reflecting does not try to calm, explain, or correct.

It names what defensiveness can feel like from the inside:
the readiness to respond, the tension of watchfulness, the sense that safety or fairness could be lost quickly. 

This poem treats defensiveness not as fault or overreaction, but as a form of protectionthat has often been learned for good reason.

There is no encouragement here to soften, forgive, or stand down.
No pressure to reframe.

Just language for recognising
what it is like to live with boundaries on high alert.

Simply read the poem and let the words land is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I feel I have to defend myself - Reflecting

There are moments when alertness arrives before thought.
A tightening. A readiness.
The sense that something needs guarding.

It may not come with clear danger.
Sometimes it appears in ordinary exchanges —
a comment, a tone, a small sense of being misunderstood.

The body responds quickly.
Boundaries draw closer.
Attention sharpens around what feels at stake.

Often, this response carries history.
Past moments where fairness was lost.
Times when standing up mattered and no one else did it for you.

Defensiveness, in this light, is not aggression.
It is an attempt to protect something valued —
dignity, autonomy, a sense of rightness.

The mind may label this reaction harshly.
Too sensitive. Too reactive. Too much.
But protection doesn’t appear without reason.
It grows where limits have been crossed,
or where crossing feels possible again.

Recognising this doesn’t remove the edge.
It doesn’t dissolve the vigilance.
It simply allows the response to be seen as meaningful,
shaped by experience,
and rooted in the wish to be treated fairly.

Seeing that can change the tone of how the moment is held,
even if nothing else changes yet.

Listening to the poem is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 30

Poem - When I feel I have to defend myself - Noticing

Over the last two days, When I feel I have to defend myself has been approached from different angles.

Day 28 worked with the body — allowing boundary reactivity to settle without collapsing firmness or clarity.

Day 29 stayed with inner experience — naming defensiveness as protection rather than fault.

Today’s poem steps back further.  When I feel I have to defend myself — Noticing
places vigilance in a wider context.

It looks at how fairness, safety, and threat are shaped relationally and socially — by power, history, expectation, and uneven consequences.

In many environments, staying alert is not optional.
Boundaries must be monitored.
Responses have weight.

Seen this way, defensiveness is not simply personal sensitivity.
It reflects conditions where what is fair or safe cannot be taken for granted.

This poem doesn’t resolve that reality.
It doesn’t offer reassurance.

It simply widens the frame, so vigilance can be understood as a response to the worlds people move through.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I feel I have to defend myself - Noticing

Many situations carry uneven power.
Decisions are made without explanation.
Rules are applied inconsistently.
Voices are weighed differently.

In such environments, alertness becomes practical.
People learn to watch closely. To notice tone, timing, implication.
To be ready before something is taken or dismissed.

Fairness is not always explicit.
It often has to be inferred, tested,
or quietly protected.

For those who have experienced being overruled, ignored, or blamed,
defensiveness can become a learned posture —
a way of staying intact in systems that do not reliably offer protection.

Modern life amplifies this.
Feedback is frequent. Judgement is public.
Boundaries are crossed quickly and often unintentionally.

In these conditions, standing guard can feel necessary.
Letting down vigilance may seem risky,
even when nothing is immediately wrong.

Seen this way, the urge to defend is not simply personal.
It reflects environments where fairness must be asserted rather than assumed.

Noticing this doesn’t lower the guard.
It doesn’t argue with the need for protection.
It simply places the experience within the structures that shape it,
where readiness is often a reasonable response to living without clear or consistent limits.

Reading the poem is enough.

Poem - When I let things slide too easily

We remain within the theme of boundaries and fairness, but today the focus shifts.

After meeting moments of vigilance and defence, today’s poem turns toward the other side of the same system — when boundaries become hard to feel at all.

Day 31 is a functional poem for times when keeping the peace comes at the cost of self-erasure, when limits soften so much they disappear.

This poem does not encourage confrontation.
It does not ask you to explain yourself, or justify where you stand.

Instead, it supports boundary presence from the inside — allowing firmness to return without aggression, pressure, or defence.

As always, nothing is required.

Poem - When I let things slide too easily

There is space here to take up the room you occupy.
Nothing needs to be given away.

The body is already present, held by its own weight, supported without leaning outward.

Awareness settles inside your outline, not drifting toward others, not scanning for approval, just noticing where you are.

Muscles gather gently, not tightening, not retreating, simply recognising their place.

Breath moves quietly, not held back, not offered forward, staying with you.

Warmth remains close, contained rather than dispersed, steady without needing to be shared.

The chest finds its own firmness, not armoured, not collapsed, able to stay upright without apology.

What belongs to you stays here. Your time. Your effort. Your limits.
The body recognises that saying nothing does not mean agreeing,
and holding ground does not require conflict.

There is a sense of being intact,
even while others move nearby,
a quiet solidity that doesn’t need permission.

This moment does not ask you to push back.
It does not ask you to explain.

You remain here, inside your own boundary,
allowed to keep what is yours without guilt.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 32

Poem - When I let things slide too easily - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked with the body — supporting boundary presence without confrontation, explanation, or defence.

Today’s poem stays with the experience of accommodation.

When I let things slide too easily — Reflecting
does not try to firm boundaries or encourage speaking up.

It names what it can feel like to smooth things over, to adapt quickly, to step aside to keep the peace.

From the inside, this pattern is often quiet.
It can feel considerate, practical, even caring.
Sometimes it’s the safest way to stay connected.

This poem treats accommodation not as weakness, but as something learned — often for good reason.

There is nothing here to change or improve.
No pressure to hold your ground.

Just language for recognising what it is like to live with boundaries that soften before you notice.

As always, nothing is required.
Reading the poem is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I let things slide too easily - Reflecting

There are times when it feels simpler not to speak.
To adjust quietly. 
To allow things to pass without comment.

Often this begins as consideration. 
A wish not to make things harder. 
A habit of smoothing the edges so others can stay comfortable.

The body may barely register the moment. 
A small tightening. A brief pause. 
Then the decision to let it go.

This can happen repeatedly, 
until yielding becomes automatic and preference fades into the background.
It’s easy, later on, to notice a vague dissatisfaction —
not sharp enough to name, but present enough to linger.

Questions may follow.
Why didn’t I say anything? 
Why do I keep agreeing? 
Why does it feel like I disappear in certain moments?

But letting things slide is rarely about weakness. 
It often grows out of care, or fear of conflict, 
or long practice in staying acceptable.

Sometimes it is the safest way learned to remain connected, 
to avoid escalation, to keep things moving.

Recognising this doesn’t restore the words not spoken. 
It doesn’t suddenly firm the boundary.

It simply allows the experience to be seen with more understanding, 
as a pattern shaped by history,

rather than a flaw of character.

Being Here - Poem Day 33

Poem - When I let things slide too easily - Noticing

Over the last two days, When I let things slide too easily has been approached from different angles.

Day 31 worked with the body — allowing boundary presence to return without confrontation or defence.

Day 32 stayed with inner experience — recognising accommodation and self-erasure as understandable ways of keeping the peace.

Today’s poem steps back further. When I let things slide too easily — Noticing places porous boundaries in a wider context.

It looks at how relationships, roles, and environments shape when accommodation feels necessary — how power, expectation, dependency, and consequence can quietly reward flexibility over firmness.

In many settings, smoothing things over is not passivity. It is how connection is preserved. It is how safety is maintained.

Seen this way, letting things slide is not a personal flaw to correct. It reflects the conditions people navigate and the costs of holding firm in certain contexts.

This poem doesn’t resolve that tension. It doesn’t suggest what should change.

It simply widens the lens, so accommodation can be understood as a response to how fairness and safety are lived, not just something happening inside one person.

As always, nothing is required.
Reading the poem is enough.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I let things slide too easily - Noticing

Many environments reward flexibility.
Adaptability is praised.
Keeping things smooth is often valued over speaking up.

In families, workplaces, and communities,
conflict can be framed as disruption,
while agreement is treated as cooperation.

Over time, this teaches subtle lessons.
That it’s easier not to object.
That harmony matters more than clarity.
That making room for others is safer than taking space.

In such contexts, boundaries can soften without being noticed.
Preferences are adjusted quietly.
Discomfort is absorbed rather than named.

This isn’t always a conscious choice.
It can become a background strategy —
a way of staying included, of avoiding escalation,
of keeping relationships intact.

For some, this pattern forms early,
in settings where fairness was uncertain or where asserting limits had consequences.

Seen this way, letting things slide is not simply personal tendency.
It reflects the conditions in which cooperation has been prioritised over self-protection.

Noticing this doesn’t harden boundaries.
It doesn’t turn accommodation into a mistake.

It simply places the experience within the systems that shape it,
where giving way can feel like the most reasonable option available at the time.

Being Here - Poem Day 34

Poem - When I swing between defending and giving in

We remain within boundaries and fairness,
and today’s poem turns toward fluctuation.

This is the movement many people recognise:
holding firm,
then giving way,
then bracing again.

Day 34 is a functional poem for moments when limits swing —
between defence and accommodation,
between standing your ground and stepping back.

This poem does not try to stabilise boundaries into one correct position.
It does not encourage confrontation
or suggest withdrawal.

Instead, it supports staying present
while boundaries tighten and soften —
allowing limits to exist
without locking or dissolving.

There is no instruction here to be consistent.
No demand to decide where you should land.

Listening is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-34.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I swing between defending and giving in

There is space here for movement without losing your ground.
Nothing needs to settle into one stance.

The body is already supported,
able to firm up and to soften without tipping too far either way.
Awareness widens to include the shift itself —
the moment of standing strong, the moment of stepping back.

Neither is treated as wrong.
Muscles adjust naturally,
not bracing for impact, not collapsing in retreat,
responding rather than reacting.

Breath continues on its own,
moving through firmness and through easing,
without choosing sides.

Warmth stays steady, not flaring outward in defence,
not fading in withdrawal, present throughout the change.
The chest does not have to harden or disappear.
It can remain responsive, meeting each moment as it arrives.

The impulse to protect is felt without being turned into attack.
The impulse to yield is felt without becoming self-erasure.
The body learns that boundaries are not fixed positions,
but living responses that can adjust without breaking.

There is a sense of staying with yourself even as limits shift,
a continuity beneath the movement.

This moment does not ask you to choose between strength and softness.
You remain here, inside a boundary that can move and hold,
protect and allow, without losing its integrity.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 35

Poem - When I swing between defending and giving in - Reflecting

Today’s poem sits alongside yesterday’s functional poem.
It doesn’t regulate or settle anything.

Instead, it stays close to a familiar inner movement:
the swing between holding firm and giving way — sometimes clear, sometimes confusing, sometimes exhausting.

This fluctuation isn’t framed as inconsistency or failure.
It’s named as something that can happen when pressure, care, and self-protection meet.

Nothing is resolved here.
Nothing is stabilised.

The poem simply offers recognition — a way of seeing the movement itself without needing to land on one side.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful; Feel the edge of where you are sitting, and stay there for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Reading is enough.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I swing between defending and giving in - Reflecting

There are moments when holding your ground feels essential.
And other moments when it feels easier to step aside.

The shift between these positions can be quick.
One situation invites firmness.
The next calls for accommodation.

From the inside, this movement can feel confusing.
Am I being too rigid? Too yielding?
Why can’t I find a middle place and stay there?

Often, both responses carry purpose.
Defending arises when something feels threatened.
Giving in appears when connection, peace, or safety feels more important.

Neither comes from nowhere.
Both are shaped by experience, by past consequences,
by what has felt possible in similar moments before.

The mind may search for consistency.
A stable rule to follow. A clear identity to inhabit.

But lived boundaries are rarely static.
They respond to context, to power, to timing,
to how much support is present.

Swinging between protecting and yielding doesn’t mean you lack clarity.
It often means you are navigating competing needs in real time.

Recognising this doesn’t resolve the movement. It doesn’t fix the oscillation.

It simply allows the experience to be seen with more honesty,
without turning it into failure or demanding it settle into one side.
