Being Here - Poem Day 36

Poem - When I swing between defending and giving in - Reflecting

Today’s poem steps back from the inner experience of boundary fluctuation and looks outward.

The movement between defending yourself and giving way doesn’t arise in isolation.It is shaped by relationships, expectations, power, timing, and the conditions people live and work within.

This poem doesn’t ask what you should do.
It doesn’t turn the swing into a personal problem to solve.

Instead, it places that movement in a wider social and relational context —
where holding firm and yielding are often responses to circumstance, not character.

Nothing is resolved here.
Nothing is corrected.

The poem simply widens the frame, allowing the experience to be seen as part of a larger pattern rather than something happening inside you alone.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful - "Look around and name where you are, quietly and simply."

Nothing else is required.

Poem - When I swing between defending and giving in - Noticing

Boundaries are not negotiated in neutral spaces.
They are shaped by roles, hierarchies, histories,
and by how much support is available in a given moment.

In some settings, firmness is required to be heard.
In others, it carries risk.
Yielding can preserve safety,
or it can quietly cost something over time.

Many people learn to adjust their boundaries in response to these conditions.
To defend when the ground feels shaky.
To give way when resistance feels too costly.

This movement is often invisible from the outside.
What looks like inconsistency may actually be responsiveness to context.

Power dynamics matter here.
So does timing.
So does whether limits have been respected in the past.

In environments where fairness is unclear or enforcement is uneven,
boundary-setting becomes a live negotiation rather than a fixed rule.

Seen this way, oscillation is not indecision.
It is a strategy — sometimes conscious, often learned —
for staying intact across changing conditions.

Noticing this doesn’t stabilise boundaries. It doesn’t prescribe the “right” response.

It simply places the experience within the realities that shape it,
where moving between defending and yielding
can be a reasonable way to navigate complex and unequal situations.

Being Here - Poem Day 37

Poem - When my worth feels tied to how much I do

Today we move into a new complex: Effort–value.

This poem works with a familiar pattern —
the sense that care, usefulness, or worth must be proven through effort, giving, or staying busy.

For many people, this pattern grows out of care rather than ego.
It carries responsibility, attentiveness, and a wish to be of value.

The poem doesn’t ask you to stop caring.
It doesn’t ask you to do less.

Instead, it quietly offers the nervous system a different possibility:
that worth can remain intact even when effort pauses —
that care does not disappear when doing settles.

There’s nothing to understand while listening.
The poem works through receptive presence alone.

Nothing else is required.

Listening is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-37.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I give more than I have

There is space here to rest without losing your value.
Nothing important is withdrawn when effort pauses.

The body is already supported,
held without needing to hold everything else,
allowed to lean back into itself.

Awareness settles where you are,
not scanning for what still needs doing,
not measuring what remains undone.

Muscles release their constant offering,
not dropping responsibility,
just setting it down for a moment.

Breath moves freely again,
no longer shaped around output,
no longer carrying quiet urgency.

Warmth stays present,
not pouring outward,
not dimming,
steady in its own place.

The chest softens without emptying.
Care doesn’t disappear —
it simply stops being spent all at once.

The urge to give is allowed to rest without being judged.
The wish to be useful remains,
but it no longer has to prove itself.

The body recognises that effort and worth are not the same thing.
There is a sense of being enough without producing,
without sustaining everything around you.

This moment does not ask you to stop caring.
It does not ask you to withdraw.

You remain here,
inside a body that can give and pause,
care and receive,
without losing its place.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 38

Poem - When I give more than I have - Reflecting

Today’s poem stays close to an experience many people recognise:
giving past capacity, continuing after something inside is already depleted.

This pattern isn’t framed as weakness or poor boundaries.
It often grows from care, responsibility, and the wish to meet what’s needed.

From the inside, over-giving can feel purposeful.
Sometimes even necessary.
Stopping may feel riskier than continuing.

The poem doesn’t ask this experience to change.
It doesn’t offer a solution or a correction.

It simply names what it can feel like to keep giving —
even when the body is asking for less —
and allows that reality to be seen without judgement.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

Notice where your body is already supported, without adding effort.

Nothing else is required.

Reading is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I give more than I have - Reflecting

There are times when giving feels like the natural response.
Seeing what’s needed,
stepping in,
offering more without being asked.

Often this comes from care.
From attentiveness.
From wanting things to go well for others.

The body may stay alert to gaps —
what hasn’t been covered,
what might fall apart,
where effort could make a difference.

Over time, this can become a pattern.
Saying yes before checking in.
Continuing past tiredness.
Measuring usefulness by how much is offered.

From the inside, it can feel purposeful.
Even meaningful.
Giving creates movement.
It keeps things flowing.

And yet, there may be a quiet cost.
A sense of being stretched thin.
Moments when exhaustion arrives before permission to stop.

It’s common, in these moments, to tell yourself this is just how you are —
reliable, generous, capable.
But generosity doesn’t erase limits.
Care doesn’t make capacity infinite.

Recognising this doesn’t undo what’s been given.
It doesn’t pull effort back.

It simply allows the experience of giving beyond what’s available to be seen honestly,
without turning it into a failure or a flaw of character.

Being Here - Poem Day 39

Poem - When I give more than I have - Noticing

Today’s poem steps back from the inner experience of over-giving and looks outward.

Giving more than is available doesn’t happen in isolation.
It is shaped by expectations, roles, timing, and by environments that quietly reward responsiveness and output.

In many settings, care is noticed most when it keeps going.
Effort is often visible.
Limits are less so.

This poem doesn’t ask whether you should give less.
It doesn’t turn over-effort into a personal failing.

Instead, it places the experience in a wider cultural and relational frame —
where being reliable, available, and helpful is often treated as proof of value.

Nothing is resolved here.
Nothing is corrected.

The poem simply widens the view, allowing over-giving to be seen as a response to conditions, not a flaw inside you.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Look around and notice where you are, right now.

Nothing else is required.

Reading is enough.

Per

Poem - When I give more than I have - Noticing

Many systems rely on people who go a little further than required.
Extra effort is often absorbed quietly.
Care is expected to stretch.

In families, workplaces, and communities,
those who notice what’s needed are often the ones who keep things moving.

Responsibility can accumulate invisibly.
What begins as choice slowly becomes assumed.
In these conditions, giving more than you have can feel necessary rather than exceptional.
Stopping may appear to risk disappointment, disruption, or loss of connection.

Cultural messages reinforce this.
Being helpful is praised.
Self-sacrifice is normalised.
Worth is subtly linked to contribution.

Over time, effort and value can blur together.
Rest begins to feel undeserved. Pausing feels like letting someone down.
Seen this way, over-giving is not simply a personal tendency.
It reflects environments that depend on unmeasured care and effort.

Noticing this doesn’t withdraw generosity.
It doesn’t argue with responsibility.
It simply places the experience within the structures that shape it,
where giving more than you have is often encouraged long before its cost is acknowledged.

Being Here - Poem Day 40

Poem - When nothing feels worth the effort

Today’s poem works with a quieter pattern in the Effort–value complex —
the sense that effort no longer carries meaning,
that value feels distant,
that doing costs more than it gives back.

This state isn’t framed as laziness or disengagement.
Often it arrives after long periods of giving, striving, or carrying responsibility.

The poem doesn’t try to motivate you.
It doesn’t argue that things matter.
It doesn’t ask you to re-engage.

Instead, it offers the nervous system a different sequence:
allowing value to be felt before effort is required —
letting worth register without needing action to prove it.

There’s nothing to understand while listening.
The poem works through receptive presence alone.

Pause.

If anything feels flat or lingering after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

    Let one moment be enough, without asking what it’s for.

Nothing else is required.

Liestening is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-40.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When nothing feels worth the effort

When nothing feels worth the effort
There is no need here to make anything matter.
Nothing is being asked of you.

The body is already present,
supported without needing to invest,
allowed to remain where it is.

Awareness settles into this moment,
not searching for purpose,
not measuring importance.

Weight rests where it falls,
not heavy,
not light,
simply there.

Breath continues quietly,
unconcerned with meaning,
arriving and leaving without demand.

Warmth appears faintly,
subtle rather than motivating,
enough to register without needing to grow.

The chest stays neutral,
neither lifted by interest
nor collapsed by disengagement.

Indifference is allowed here.
So is weariness.
Neither needs to be corrected.

The body recognises that value
does not always announce itself as desire or urgency.

Sometimes worth is felt first as simple presence —
being here without wanting more.
This moment does not ask you to care harder.
It does not ask you to try again.

You remain here,
inside a body that can rest until something feels worth meeting,
in its own time.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 41

Poem - When nothing feels worth the effort - Reflecting

Today’s poem stays with a quieter experience —
the sense that effort no longer carries weight,
that doing doesn’t seem to lead anywhere meaningful.

This state isn’t framed as apathy or failure.
It often follows long periods of giving, striving, or responding to demand.

From the inside, disengagement can feel protective.
Pulling back may be the body’s way of conserving what remains.

The poem doesn’t try to shift this experience.
It doesn’t offer purpose or encouragement.

It simply names what it can feel like
when value feels distant
and effort feels like too much.

Nothing is being corrected here.
Nothing needs to be overcome.

The poem offers recognition —
a way of seeing this state without judgement or urgency.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels heavy after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Notice where your body is already being held.

Nothing else is required.

Poem - When nothing feels worth the effort - Reflecting

There are times when interest fades quietly.
Not in a dramatic way, but as a gradual thinning of motivation.

Tasks remain. Options exist.
Yet none of them seem to carry enough weight to draw you toward them.

From the outside, this can look like apathy.
A lack of ambition.
A reluctance to engage.

From the inside, it often feels different.
More like exhaustion. Or disappointment.
Or having spent energy without seeing it return.

Effort asks a question: Is this worth it?
And sometimes the answer,
honestly felt, is simply no — not right now.

This can be unsettling.
Especially in cultures that equate effort with character,
and engagement with virtue.

It’s easy, in these moments,
to turn the absence of motivation into self-criticism —
to assume something essential has been lost.

But disengagement doesn’t always mean disinterest.
It can signal that meaning has been stretched thin,
that reward has not matched what was given,
or that rest has been overdue.

Recognising this doesn’t restore desire.
It doesn’t make things suddenly appealing.

It simply allows the experience of not finding things worth the effort to be seen without judgement,
as part of how value ebbs and flows over time.

Being Here - Poem Day 42

Poem - When nothing feels worth the effort - Noticing

Today’s poem steps back from inner experience and looks outward.

Low motivation and disengagement don’t arise only from within.
They are shaped by environments where effort is expected to be constant,
where rewards are delayed or uneven, and where rest is often treated as secondary.

In many lives, effort is asked for repeatedly
without clear completion or return.Over time, value can begin to feel abstract —
something promised rather than felt.

This poem doesn’t ask whether you should try harder.
It doesn’t turn disengagement into a personal problem to solve.

Instead, it places the experience in a wider cultural and structural context —
where withdrawing effort can be a reasonable response
to conditions that offer little sense of “enough.”

Nothing is resolved here.
Nothing is reframed.

The poem simply widens the view,
allowing low valuation to be seen as something that happens in worlds like this,
not as something wrong inside you.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels heavy after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Look around and notice where you are, right now.

Nothing else is required.

Reading is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When nothing feels worth the effort - Noticing

Many systems assume that effort will be met with reward.
Time given will lead somewhere.
Energy spent will return as satisfaction, progress, or security.

But this isn’t always how things unfold.
Work can be repeated without recognition.
Care can be offered without relief.
Effort can disappear into structures that don’t respond.

In such conditions, motivation doesn’t fade by accident.
It erodes gradually,
shaped by experiences where giving more did not change what mattered.

Modern life often accelerates this.
Outcomes are delayed or abstract.
Success is measured indirectly.
Reward is promised, then postponed.

When effort stops feeling worthwhile,
it can look like disengagement.
But it may also be a form of discernment — a system noticing that the exchange is no longer balanced.

Seen this way, low motivation is not simply lack.
It reflects environments where value is unclear,
or where effort has been repeatedly disconnected from what feels meaningful.

Noticing this doesn’t restore interest.
It doesn’t create desire.

It simply places the experience within the wider conditions that shape value,
where pulling back effort can be a reasonable response to a world that hasn’t given much back.

 

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-42.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

Being Here - Poem Day 43

Poem - When effort rises and falls

Today’s poem works with a familiar movement:
periods of energy and engagement followed by withdrawal.
Wanting to give, then needing to step back.

This pattern isn’t framed as inconsistency.
It often reflects changing capacity, uneven return, or the natural rise and fall of energy.

The poem doesn’t ask you to stabilise.
It doesn’t suggest recommitment or renewed effort.

Instead, it offers the nervous system something quieter:
that worth can remain steady even as effort changes —
that value does not increase when you give
or decrease when you pause.

There’s nothing to work out while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything feels unsettled or lingering after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let one shift in energy happen without adjusting your view of yourself.

Nothing else is required.

Listening is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-43.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When effort rises and falls

There is room here for giving and for stopping. Nothing needs to stay the same.
The body is already supported, able to lean in and to lean back without losing its place.
Awareness widens to include the shift — the moment of engagement, the moment of retreat, both arriving honestly.

Energy gathers for a while, then softens. Neither is treated as failure.
Breath continues on its own, moving through effort and through rest, without preference.
Warmth adjusts gently, sometimes more available, sometimes quieter, remaining present throughout.

The chest does not have to decide. It can stay responsive, meeting each phase as it comes.
The urge to contribute is allowed without being turned into obligation. The urge to withdraw is allowed without becoming absence.

The body recognises that value is not measured by how steadily effort is given.
There is a sense of being intact through movement and pause, inside the same steady outline.
This moment does not ask you to recommit or to step away.

You remain here, inside a body that can offer and rest, engage and recover, without losing its worth.

Being Here - Poem Day 44

Poem - When effort rises and falls - Reflecting

Today’s poem stays with a familiar fluctuation —
times of energy and engagement followed by periods of retreat.

From the inside, this movement can feel unpredictable.

At one moment there is willingness, direction, even momentum.
At another, effort feels distant or unnecessary.
It’s easy to interpret this shift as inconsistency.
To wonder which version is the “real” one.

But fluctuation often reflects capacity rather than character.
Energy responds to context, return, fatigue, and timing.

The poem doesn’t try to stabilise this movement.
It doesn’t suggest choosing one side over the other.

It simply names what it can feel like
when effort rises and falls —
without turning the change into a problem to fix.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.
   Notice where your body is already supported.
Nothing else is required.

Listening is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When effort rises and falls - Reflecting

There are times when energy feels available and easy to offer. Interest appears. Care moves outward. Effort feels aligned.

And then, just as naturally, it recedes. What felt worth engaging with loses its pull. Rest becomes more compelling than contribution.

This shift can be unsettling. Especially when there’s an expectation that motivation should be reliable, that once something matters, it should continue to matter in the same way.

The mind may search for explanation. Am I losing interest? Am I giving up too soon? Should I push through this?

But effort does not always move in straight lines. It responds to capacity, to meaning, to whether care has been met or depleted.

Sometimes the withdrawal is protective. A response to having given without pause. Sometimes it signals that something needs to change, or simply to wait.

Oscillation can feel like inconsistency, but it can also be sensitivity — a system adjusting in real time to what feels possible.

Recognising this doesn’t smooth the rhythm. It doesn’t stabilise motivation.

It simply allows the movement itself to be named without judgement, as part of how effort and value find their balance over time.

Being Here - Poem Day 45

Poem - When effort rises and falls - Noticing

Today’s poem steps back from the personal experience of fluctuation and places it in a wider frame.

In many environments, consistency is rewarded.
Steady output is easier to measure.
Linear progress is easier to recognise.

Within those structures, rising and falling effort can appear irregular — even problematic.

But human energy rarely moves in straight lines.
Engagement responds to return, context, fatigue, reciprocity, and meaning.
Systems are often organised around constancy; bodies are not.

Today’s poem doesn’t turn inward.
It doesn’t try to stabilise the rhythm.

It simply places fluctuating effort within the cultural and structural patterns many of us live inside.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Look around and notice one steady object in the room.

Nothing else is required.

Listening is enough.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When effort rises and falls - Noticing

Many systems assume steady contribution. Effort is expected to be consistent. Engagement is treated as reliable rather than responsive.

Yet most environments are uneven. Demand changes quickly. Reward arrives late, indirectly, or not at all.

In such conditions, effort often becomes cyclical. People lean in when something feels meaningful. They pull back when energy has been spent without return.

This movement is rarely acknowledged. Instead, constancy is praised, while fluctuation is framed as a lack of commitment.

Modern life reinforces this pattern. Opportunities multiply. Expectations expand. Rest is treated as interruption rather than necessity.

Within these structures, rising and falling effort can be a form of calibration — a system testing how much to give, and when to conserve.

Seen this way, oscillation is not inefficiency. It is adjustment. A response to environments that do not pace themselves.

Noticing this doesn’t stabilise motivation. It doesn’t instruct effort to return.

It simply places the experience within the realities that shape it, where offering energy intermittently may be the most sustainable way to stay engaged at all.

Being Here - Poem Day 46

Poem - When I’m always measuring where I stand

Today’s poem works with a particular kind of vigilance —
the sense of being measured, compared, or evaluated.

This can show up as pressure to prove,
to hold position,
to avoid slipping in standing.

The nervous system can treat status as safety.
Rank can feel tied to belonging, security, or future opportunity.

The poem does not ask you to give up ambition.
It does not question competence or drive.

Instead, it offers something quieter:

that position may shift,
but worth does not relocate with it.

Nothing needs to be demonstrated while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

Feel the support beneath your feet and remain there for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-46.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I’m always measuring where I stand

There is space here to stop checking for a moment. Nothing is being assessed right now.

The body is already supported, held without needing to rise or fall, steady without climbing.

Awareness settles into where you are, not scanning above or below, not tracking who is ahead or behind.

Muscles release their quiet readiness, not losing strength, just easing the constant comparison.

Breath moves freely again, no longer shaped by anticipation, no longer preparing for judgement.

Warmth stays close and contained, not surging to impress, not withdrawing to hide.

The chest remains upright without strain, not puffed up, not shrinking back, able to hold itself.

The sense of value gathers inward, less dependent on reflection, less tied to how you appear.

The body recognises that position can change without threatening existence.

There is a feeling of standing on your own ground, not ranked, not evaluated, simply present.

This moment does not ask you to improve your place. It does not ask you to lower yourself.

You remain here, inside a body that knows its worth without needing to compare, without needing to prove.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 47

Poem - When I’m always measuring where I stand - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked quietly with status vigilance —
the pressure to prove, maintain position, or avoid slipping in standing.

Today’s poem stays closer to the inner experience of that movement.

Comparison can happen quickly.
A room is entered.
A conversation unfolds.
Attention scans — who is confident, who is influential, where do I stand?

This vigilance is not necessarily competitive.
Often, it is adaptive.

For many people, position has mattered —
for safety, for belonging, for opportunity.Learning to read hierarchy can be a way of staying oriented in systems where rank influences outcome.

Today’s poem does not attempt to calm this.
It does not ask comparison to stop.

It simply names what it can feel like
to live inside that constant measuring —
without turning it into a flaw.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Notice one thing in the room that is not evaluating you.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,
Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I’m always measuring where I stand - Reflecting

There are moments when awareness turns outward automatically. Who is ahead. Who is behind. Where you seem to fit in the picture.

Comparison can arrive quietly. A glance. A thought. A subtle recalculation of place.

Often this happens without intention. The mind scans for cues — tone, recognition, response — looking for signs of standing or slipping.

This vigilance rarely comes from vanity alone. It is often shaped by environments where position mattered, where being seen correctly affected safety, opportunity, or belonging.

Staying alert once served a purpose. It helped you adapt. It helped you learn the rules. It helped you avoid falling too far out of view.

Over time, this scanning can become constant. Even in neutral spaces. Even when nothing is being asked.

The body may carry this as tension. A readiness to adjust. A need to stay one step ahead of judgement.

It’s easy to judge this habit harshly. To see it as insecurity or unnecessary self-focus.

But measuring where you stand is often an attempt to stay oriented in systems that don’t make status explicit.

Recognising this doesn’t stop the comparison. It doesn’t remove the habit.

It simply allows the experience to be seen as a learned response, shaped by context, rather than a personal failing.

Performance is tracked.

Poem - When I’m always measuring where I stand - Noticing

Many environments are organised around ranking, even when it isn’t openly named.

Roles come with invisible ladders. Recognition is unevenly distributed. Attention flows toward some positions and away from others.

In such settings, comparison becomes practical. People learn to read signals — who is listened to, who is deferred to, who is overlooked.

Status is rarely stable. It can shift with context, with performance, with who is present in the room.

This instability encourages vigilance. Staying alert feels necessary when position can change without warning.

Modern life intensifies this further. Metrics are public. Achievements are displayed. Visibility is continuous.

Within these conditions, measuring where you stand is not simply personal insecurity. It reflects systems that invite comparison as a way of organising value.

Noticing this doesn’t remove the urge to compare. It doesn’t resolve the tension around status.

It simply places the experience within the structures that shape it, where keeping track of position can feel like a reasonable response to living in hierarchies that rarely rest.

Being Here - Poem Day 49

Poem - When I make myself smaller

Earlier in this complex, we worked with status vigilance —
the pressure to prove, to hold position, to avoid slipping.

Today’s poem moves in the opposite direction.

Sometimes the response to hierarchy is not striving upward,
but staying low.
Reducing presence.
Taking up less space to remain safe.

This can be subtle.
Quieter voice.
Less eye contact.
Letting others move ahead.

For many people, this has been adaptive.
In some environments, shrinking reduced risk.

The poem does not ask you to become dominant.
It does not push toward confidence or exposure.

Instead, it works with something simpler:

that occupying your space quietly
does not create danger.

That vertical presence and dignity
do not require performance.

There is nothing to achieve while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your spine lengthen slightly and remain there for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I make myself smaller

There is space here to be the size you are. Nothing needs to be reduced.

The body is already supported, held by what’s beneath it, allowed to rise without lifting itself.

Awareness settles inside your outline, not shrinking back, not pressing forward, just noticing your place.

Muscles gather gently, not to defend, not to retreat, simply to hold you upright.

Breath moves easily again, not hidden, not restrained, moving through your whole shape.

Warmth stays present, not dimmed, not withdrawn, steady and contained.

The chest finds its own height, not puffed up, not folded inward, able to exist without apology.

The sense of being seen does not require performance. Visibility does not have to be earned.

The body recognises that taking up space does not threaten anyone.

There is a feeling of being here, noticeable without effort, solid without display.

This moment does not ask you to stand out or step aside.

You remain here, inside a body that is allowed to occupy its place without shrinking.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 50

Poem - When I make myself smaller - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked quietly with taking up space —
without dominance, without performance.

Today’s poem stays closer to the inner experience of shrinking.

Self-minimising can be subtle.
Lowering volume.
Holding back an opinion.
Letting others move ahead.

From the outside, this can look like modesty or flexibility.

From the inside, it may feel like calibration.

In some environments, being visible carried cost.
Standing out meant scrutiny.
Attention meant evaluation.

Over time, stepping back can become automatic —
a way of maintaining safety, harmony, or stability.

Today’s poem does not ask you to expand.
It does not suggest confidence or exposure.

It simply recognises
that staying smaller
has often been a learned survival strategy.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Notice the outline of your body where it meets the chair.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,
Per

Poem - When I make myself smaller - Reflecting

There are moments when staying unnoticed feels safer. Lowering your voice. Reducing your presence. Letting others take the lead.

Often this happens quietly. A habit rather than a decision. A way of moving through spaces without attracting attention.

For some, this began early. In environments where standing out invited criticism, or where taking space felt risky.

Making yourself smaller can be protective. It avoids conflict. It limits exposure. It keeps things manageable.

Over time, this adjustment can become familiar. Comfortable even. Visibility begins to feel like pressure rather than opportunity.

The cost may only appear later. A sense of being overlooked. Of contributions going unseen. Of having more to offer than is shown.

It’s easy to judge this pattern harshly. To wish it were different. To push yourself to be louder or bolder.

But self-minimising is not weakness. It is often intelligence — a response shaped by context, by experience, by what once worked.

Recognising this doesn’t suddenly change how much space you take. It doesn’t force visibility.

It simply allows the experience of making yourself smaller to be understood with more compassion, as a way of staying safe in a world that hasn’t always welcomed presence.

Being Here - Poem Day 51

Poem - When I make myself smaller - Noticing

Over the past two days, we’ve stayed close to the experience of shrinking —
first through the body, then through inner recognition.

Today’s poem steps outward.

Self-minimising does not happen in isolation.
It often unfolds inside systems where space is not evenly distributed.

Some voices are amplified.
Some are expected to defer.
Some learn early that visibility carries risk.

Cultural norms can value modesty.
Groups can settle into roles.
Histories can shape who stands forward and who remains at the edges.

Within these structures, reducing one’s presence may not reflect lack of worth.
It may reflect adaptation.

Today’s poem does not turn inward.
It does not suggest taking more space.

It simply places invisibility within broader social and historical patterns.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your eyes rest on something in the room that takes up space without apology.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

Poem - When I make myself smaller - Noticing

Many spaces are not neutral about presence. Some voices are welcomed. Others are tolerated. Some are quietly overlooked.

In such environments, visibility carries risk. Being noticed can invite scrutiny, comparison, or consequence.

People learn quickly where it is safer to stand. Who can speak freely. Who should stay cautious. Who benefits from being seen.

Hierarchy doesn’t always announce itself. It operates through tone, through attention, through who is interrupted and who is listened to.

In these conditions, making yourself smaller can be a practical adaptation. A way of staying included without drawing attention.

This pattern is often reinforced. Quiet cooperation is rewarded. Loud presence is questioned. Staying unobtrusive feels safer than misstepping.

Seen this way, self-minimising is not simply lack of confidence. It reflects environments where presence has not been evenly supported.

Noticing this doesn’t expand your space. It doesn’t encourage visibility.

It simply places the experience within the structures that shape it, where shrinking back can feel like the most reasonable response available.

Being Here - Poem Day 52

Poem - When I move between standing out and disappearing

In the last two days, we explored two directions of Emotional Complex 6 (Status & hierarchy):

- striving to hold position, when it is over-activated
- shrinking to stay safe, when it is under-activated

Today’s poem works with something more subtle —
the movement between them, when it is oscillating.

There can be days of visibility.
Energy forward.
Voice steady.

And then days of withdrawal.
Silence.
Distance.
Reduced presence.

This fluctuation does not always feel intentional.
It can feel unpredictable.

The nervous system may treat this oscillation as instability —
as if presence must be fixed to be safe.

Today’s poem does not push confidence.
It does not promote humility.
It does not ask for consistency.

Instead, it offers something steadier:

that presence can change shape without becoming fragile.

That stepping forward and stepping back can both belong.

Nothing needs to be decided while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your feet feel the ground beneath them for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

Poem - When I move between standing out and disappearing

There is space here to be seen and to step back. Nothing needs to settle into one position.

The body is already supported, able to rise into view and to ease back without losing its ground.

Awareness widens to include the movement — the moment of stepping forward, the moment of retreat, both held equally.

Muscles adjust naturally, not bracing to perform, not collapsing to hide, responding to what’s needed.

Breath continues without preference, moving through exposure and through privacy, steady throughout.

Warmth stays present, not flaring to impress, not dimming to disappear, contained and reliable.

The chest doesn’t have to commit to being open or closed. It can remain responsive, meeting each moment as it arrives.

The impulse to show yourself is allowed without becoming display. The impulse to withdraw is allowed without becoming erasure.

The body learns that visibility and rest can alternate without threatening worth.

There is a sense of staying with yourself through appearing and receding, a continuity beneath the change.

This moment does not ask you to choose how much space to take.

You remain here, inside a body that can appear and step back, be noticed and be private, without losing its place.

For now, that is enough.

Day 53 — When I move between standing out and disappearing (Reflecting)

Yesterday’s poem worked directly with oscillation —

Today’s poem stays closer to the inner experience of that movement.

There are times when visibility feels natural.
Speech steady.
Energy present.

And other times when something shifts.
Silence grows.
Presence recedes.

This fluctuation can be confusing.

Was one version more authentic?
Should consistency be possible?

Often, the movement is not deliberate.
It may reflect sensitivity to context,
to tone,
to subtle cues about what feels permitted.

Wanting to be seen and wanting to stay protected
can coexist.

Oscillation, in this light,
is not necessarily instability.

It may be a way of navigating spaces
where visibility carries both invitation and risk.

Today’s poem does not ask for steadiness.
It does not suggest choosing one version to keep.

It simply names the movement.

Poem - When I move between standing out and disappearing - Reflecting

There are moments when being seen feels right. When speaking up feels natural. When presence carries energy rather than risk.

And then, just as clearly, there are moments when pulling back feels safer. When quiet feels protective. When being less visible brings relief.

The movement between these states can be subtle. A shift in who is present. A change in tone. A sense that the ground has altered.

From the inside, this can feel inconsistent. Why do I show up fully here and disappear there? Why does confidence come and go?

Often, both responses are sensible. Visibility carries opportunity. Withdrawal reduces exposure. Each serves a different need.

The body may respond before the mind catches up. Leaning forward when it feels supported. Stepping back when the cost feels higher.

It’s easy to judge this movement. To wish for steadiness. To want a single, reliable way of being.

But lived presence is rarely fixed. It adjusts to context, to power, to how welcome visibility feels.

Recognising this doesn’t stop the shifting. It doesn’t lock presence into one form.

It simply allows the experience of moving between standing out and disappearing to be seen with more understanding, as a responsive pattern rather than a personal flaw.

Being Here - Poem Day 55

Poem — When I feel responsible for everyone

We now move into a new complex: Contribution / caregiving.

For some, care expresses itself not as choice,
but as urgency.

A quick noticing of what is needed.
A readiness to fix.
A sense that someone must step in — and that someone is you.

This pattern often grows from care itself.
From empathy.
From wanting others to be well.

Over time, though, responsibility can become automatic.
The body may lean forward before a request is spoken.

Today’s poem works with that urgency.

It does not withdraw care.
It does not suggest indifference.
It does not reduce compassion.

Instead, it offers something steadier:

that care can remain present
without self-erasure.

That you can stay whole
while still facing outward.

Nothing needs to be decided while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

Let your shoulders drop slightly and remain there for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

Poem - When I feel responsible for everyone

There is space here to care without carrying everything. Nothing is falling apart if you pause.

The body is already supported, held without holding others up, steady without leaning outward.

Awareness settles into where you are, not scanning for who needs you next, not listening for distress at a distance.

Muscles release their constant readiness, not abandoning strength, just setting down what is not yours.

Breath moves freely again, no longer shaped around vigilance, no longer braced for urgency.

Warmth stays close and contained, not pouring outward to fix, not dimming, present without rushing.

The chest softens without collapsing. Care doesn’t disappear — it simply stops running ahead.

The urge to help is allowed without being acted on immediately. Concern can exist without becoming responsibility.

The body recognises that others have weight of their own, paths of their own, capacity that does not depend on you.

There is a sense of being available without being consumed, present without being required.

This moment does not ask you to stop caring. It does not ask you to harden.
You remain here, inside a body that can care and rest, offer and remain intact, without losing itself.

For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 56

Poem — When I feel responsible for everyone - Reflecting

Yesterday’s poem worked directly with caregiving urgency —
the reflex to step in, to fix, to carry.

Today’s poem stays closer to the inner experience of that responsibility.

For some, noticing needs happens quickly.
Attention moves outward almost automatically.

Responsibility can feel less like choice
and more like calibration.

If someone is unsettled,
the body registers it.
If something might go wrong,
the mind prepares.

Over time, usefulness can become stabilising.
Being needed can feel like belonging.

In this light, over-responsibility is not simply overextension.
It may be a meaningful adaptation —
a way of maintaining connection, preventing harm, or securing place.

Today’s poem does not ask you to step back.
It does not question your care.

It simply names what this pattern can feel like from the inside.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your back rest fully against the chair for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I feel responsible for everyone - Reflecting

There are moments when attention turns outward almost automatically. Who is struggling. Who might need support. What could be done to help.

Caring can feel instinctive. A way of staying connected. A way of making sense of your place among others.

Often, this responsiveness has a history. Times when stepping in mattered.

Moments when help wasn’t optional. Experiences where being needed created belonging.

Over time, concern can become constant. The body stays alert to signals of distress. Rest feels conditional, earned only once everyone else is settled.

From the inside, this can feel purposeful. Responsible. Even loving.

And yet, there may be a quiet cost. A sense of being stretched thin. Of carrying more than was ever meant to be carried.

It can be hard to tell where care ends and responsibility begins. Harder still to imagine letting go without something important being lost.

But caring deeply does not require holding everything together. Responsibility does not have to be total in order to be real.

Recognising this doesn’t loosen the habit. It doesn’t remove the pull to help.

It simply allows the experience of feeling responsible for everyone to be seen with more honesty, as an expression of care that may have grown beyond its original bounds.

Being Here - Poem Day 57

Day 57 — When I feel responsible for everyone - Noticing

Earlier in this complex, we worked directly with caregiving urgency —
the reflex to step in, to hold, to manage.

Yesterday, we stayed close to the inner experience of that responsibility.

Today’s poem steps outward.

Over-responsibility does not develop in isolation.

In many families, roles form early —
the reliable one, the stabiliser, the one who notices first.

In workplaces, those who are competent and attentive
often receive more informal care tasks.

In wider culture, self-sacrifice is frequently praised.
Helping more can be equated with caring more.

Within such structures, caregiving urgency may not feel excessive.
It may feel aligned with what is valued.

This poem does not ask you to reduce your care.
It does not reassign responsibility.

It simply places over-responsibility
within the relational and cultural patterns
where it often gathers.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your hands rest without holding anything for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I feel responsible for everyone - Noticing

Many roles quietly reward taking on more than is named. Care is often assumed rather than negotiated. Responsibility expands without clear boundaries.

In families, workplaces, and communities, those who notice what’s needed are often relied upon without being asked. Support becomes expected. Availability becomes invisible labour.

Cultural stories reinforce this. Being dependable is praised. Putting others first is admired. Exhaustion is sometimes mistaken for virtue.

In such contexts, responsibility can spread outward, filling gaps left by systems that don’t adequately hold people. Care steps in where structure is thin.

Over time, this shapes how contribution is lived. The line between helping and holding becomes blurred. Concern turns into obligation.

Seen this way, feeling responsible for everyone is not simply personal tendency. It reflects environments that rely on unspoken caregiving to keep things functioning.

Noticing this doesn’t remove compassion. It doesn’t withdraw care.

It simply places the experience within the conditions that encourage it, where taking on too much can feel like the only way to keep things from falling apart.

Being Here - Poem Day 58

Day 58 — When I have nothing left to give

Earlier in this complex, we worked with caregiving urgency —
the reflex to step in, to hold, to manage.

Today’s poem moves in the opposite direction.

There are times when care feels quiet.
Energy feels thin.
The impulse to respond simply isn’t there.

This can be unsettling.

In cultures that value generosity,
reduced care can be interpreted as failure.
As withdrawal.
As not being enough.

But exhaustion is not indifference.

Sometimes care recedes
because it has been extended for a long time.

Today’s poem does not ask you to give.
It does not ask you to feel warmth.
It does not push compassion to return.

Instead, it honours rested care.

It allows the absence of urgency
without turning it into guilt.

Nothing needs to be produced while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

Let your hands rest open and still for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_audio playback_speed="off" loop="off" autoplay="off" preload="none" box_shadow="no" box_shadow_blur="0" box_shadow_spread="0" animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" src="https://deepermindfulness.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Poem_Being-Here-Poem-Day-58.mp3" /][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 

Poem - When I don’t feel able to give

There is no requirement here to offer anything. Nothing is missing because you are resting.

The body is already supported, held without needing to extend itself, allowed to remain gathered.

Awareness settles into where you are, not reaching outward, not checking who needs you, just staying close.


Muscles soften from holding others in mind, not giving up care, just releasing the strain of carrying.


Breath moves quietly, uninvolved, arriving and leaving without expectation.


Warmth stays present, subtle rather than expansive, enough to be felt without being spent.


The chest remains steady. It does not need to open. It does not need to close.


Exhaustion is allowed here. So is numbness. Neither is judged.


The body recognises that care cannot flow when it has nowhere to rest.


There is a sense of being intact without contributing, whole without giving.


This moment does not ask you to recover quickly or to become available again.


You remain here, inside a body that can pause, so that care may return when there is room.


For now, that is enough.

Being Here - Poem Day 59

Day 59 — When I don’t feel able to give (Reflecting)

Yesterday’s poem worked directly with exhaustion —
honouring rested care rather than forced giving.

Today’s poem stays closer to the inner experience of that quiet.

There are moments when the instinct to help feels muted.
When empathy does not rise in the way it once did.
When stepping back feels easier than stepping in.

This can be confusing.
Especially if care has long been part of how you understand yourself.

From the outside, it may look like withdrawal.
From the inside, it can feel like depletion.
Or numbness.
Or simply having reached a limit.

Not feeling able to give is not necessarily indifference. It may reflect a system that has carried more than it could sustain.

Today’s poem does not ask for recovery.
It does not urge generosity.
It does not frame rest as something to overcome.

It simply names the experience.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your feet rest fully on the floor for a moment.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 Poem 59 - When I don’t feel able to give - Reflecting

There are times when the capacity to care feels distant. Not gone, but unreachable.

The wish to help may still be there in theory, yet the energy to respond doesn’t follow. What once felt natural now feels heavy.

This can be confusing. Especially for those who are used to being available, attentive, responsive to others’ needs.

The mind may search for explanations. Am I burned out? Have I become selfish? Why does giving feel so difficult now?

Often, what’s present is not lack of care, but depletion. A long period of offering without enough space to recover.

Care does not disappear when it pauses. It retreats when there is nowhere left to land. When rest has been postponed too long. When giving has outpaced receiving.

In these moments, stepping back can feel like loss of identity. If I’m not helping, who am I?

But the capacity to give has its own rhythm. It cannot be demanded back into place.

Recognising this doesn’t restore energy. It doesn’t make care immediately available again.

It simply allows the experience of not being able to give to be seen without blame, as part of how caregiving naturally ebbs and flows.

Being Here - Poem Day 60

Day 60 — When I don’t feel able to give (Noticing)

Earlier in this sequence, we worked with exhaustion directly —
honouring rested care rather than forcing generosity.

Yesterday, we stayed close to the inner experience of withdrawal.

Today’s poem steps outward.

Compassion fatigue does not develop in isolation.

In many environments, demand outpaces capacity.
Roles multiply without pause.
Crisis becomes continuous.
Resources thin.

Where urgency is sustained and recovery is limited,
responsiveness may narrow.

This does not necessarily signal indifference.
It may reflect structural strain.

Care requires margin —
of time,
of energy,
of safety.

When margin is reduced,
withdrawal can follow.

Today’s poem does not ask for renewal.
It does not encourage generosity.

It simply places caregiving fatigue
within the broader systems
where responsibility often exceeds what is sustainable.

Pause.

If anything lingers after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let your gaze rest on something that is not asking anything of you.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

[/fusion_text][fusion_text animation_direction="left" animation_speed="0.3" animation_delay="0" hide_on_mobile="small-visibility,medium-visibility,large-visibility" sticky_display="normal,sticky"]

 Poem 60 - When I don’t feel able to give - Noticing

Care is often treated as an endless resource. Those who give are expected to keep giving. Limits are rarely discussed until they are reached.


In many roles, stepping back is not clearly supported. Rest is allowed only after exhaustion. Pauses are justified rather than assumed.


Systems frequently depend on personal care to fill gaps in structure, time, and support. When that care falters, the strain becomes visible.


In such conditions, withdrawal is not surprising. It is often the only remaining signal that something has been overextended.


Compassion fatigue is not a lack of heart. It reflects prolonged exposure to need without sufficient recovery. To giving without adequate receiving.


Modern life compounds this. Crises overlap. Demands accumulate. There is little space between one call for care and the next.


Seen this way, not feeling able to give is not a personal failing. It reflects environments that do not reliably protect those who care.


Noticing this doesn’t restore capacity. It doesn’t demand resilience.


It simply places the experience within the realities that shape it, where stepping back may be the most reasonable response to having given for too long without rest.

Being Here - Poem Day 61

Day 61 — When I move between giving and needing distance

Across the last few days we explored two ends of the caregiving spectrum.

First, the urgency to help —
stepping in quickly, carrying more than your share.

Then the opposite experience —
exhaustion, compassion fatigue, the sense of having nothing left to give.

Today’s poem works with something many people recognise:

movement between the two.

There can be periods of strong care —
energy, attentiveness, generosity.

Then something shifts.
Distance becomes necessary.
Quiet replaces urgency.

From the outside this can look inconsistent.

From the inside it may simply reflect how energy moves.

Today’s poem does not ask for balance.
It does not push generosity to return.
It does not suggest holding back.

Instead, it allows care to move.

Giving and distance can both exist
without either cancelling the other.

Nothing needs to be stabilised while listening.
The sequence carries itself.

Pause.

If anything lingers or feels activating after listening, you might try one small thing — only if it feels helpful.

   Let one breath finish fully before the next begins.

Nothing else is required.

Warmly,

Per

 Poem 61 - When I move between giving and pulling back

There is space here for care to come and go. Nothing needs to settle into one role.

The body is already supported, able to lean outward and to return to itself without losing its ground.

Awareness widens to include the movement — the impulse to offer, the need to pause, both held without judgement.

Muscles adjust gently, not bracing to help, not collapsing to rest, responding as capacity shifts.

Breath continues freely, moving through giving and through withdrawal, without choosing sides.

Warmth flows and gathers, sometimes extending, sometimes staying close, remaining present throughout.

The chest does not have to decide how available to be. It can stay responsive, meeting each moment as it arrives.

The urge to help is allowed without becoming obligation. The urge to step back is allowed without becoming absence.

The body learns that care does not disappear when it rests, and does not lose itself when it moves outward.

There is a sense of staying intact through offering and retreat, inside the same steady outline.

This moment does not ask you to commit to giving or to withdraw completely.

You remain here, inside a body that can care and pause, respond and recover, without losing its heart.

For now, that is enough.
